source.title: Quadratic integrate-and-fire neurons exhibit less fragmented loss landscapes and outperform leaky integrate-and-fire neurons in spike-based gradient descent
source.authors: Carlo Wenig; Raoul-Martin Memmesheimer; Christian Klos

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains and analyzes spiking neural networks, an application setting outside the listed claim versions, and reports its own training outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training accuracy and analyses loss and gradient landscapes for its own networks. It does not test CIFAR training, random or corrupted labels, two-layer ReLU teacher-student minima, depth with shortcuts, initialization effects, learning-rate stability limits, or batch normalization.
record.test_reason: The study compares QIF and LIF spiking networks on SHD. None of its results tests V1–V6: training accuracy concerns different systems and data, landscape fragmentation is not evidence of spurious local minima, and gradient predictiveness is not learning-rate stability. Residual connections and batch normalization appear in related work; Kaiming initialization is used without testing V4's mechanism or outcomes.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that QIF networks outperform LIF networks in this SHD setting and that continuous spiking dynamics appear practically advantageous. They recommend considering continuous-dynamics neurons for gradient training, while explicitly leaving generalization to other tasks, coding schemes, neuron/input settings and surrogate gradients unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses exact spike-based gradient descent on time-continuous spiking networks and SHD, rather than the ANN recipes and benchmarks in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance and training behavior differ between QIF and LIF neurons, and between the best-performing and asynchronous LIF configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Final training accuracies for the selected QIF, best LIF and asynchronous LIF networks were 97.0%, 83.5% and 45.6%; larger exploratory QIF and LIF networks reached 99.973% and 94.08%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested SHD recipes with exact spike-based gradients and Adam, the selected QIF networks attain higher training accuracy than the compared LIF networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Actual loss decreased in 90%, 75% and 62% of steps predicting a decrease for QIF, best LIF and asynchronous LIF, respectively, in one trajectory per configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: First-order loss predictions are more reliable along the tested QIF training trajectory than along the compared LIF trajectories.

fits_no_version.finding: The fraction of gradient components zero across all samples within an epoch reaches about 62% for asynchronous LIF and about 25% for best LIF and QIF.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested asynchronous LIF configuration has more inactive gradient components than the best LIF and QIF configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Landscape visualizations show more severe fragmentation for LIF, including loss discontinuities; QIF loss transitions remain continuous, although its gradients can be discontinuous.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the examined SHD networks and parameter slices, QIF dynamics yield less fragmented loss and gradient landscapes than LIF dynamics.

record.problems: The authors focus on a single task and output coding scheme, and only consider intrinsically oscillating neurons with input currents that cause jumps directly in membrane potential. They state that extension to other settings remains future work. Hyperparameter selection used the test set, which the authors acknowledge may overestimate test accuracy. The final training-accuracy results are reported for 10 seeds in Table 1 and 9 runs in Table 2.

untested.parts: All: convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, clean or corrupted labels, and training-error dependence on size and training recipe.
All: ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
All: depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization and normalization exceptions.
All: activation-matched initialization preserving signal and gradient propagation, training speed and depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
All: recovery or divergence relative to an initial stability limit, curvature reduction, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
All: batch normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: A new application setting alone does not justify T3 when no claim version is tested. The initialization-scale search reports selected test accuracies, without establishing V4's propagation, speed or depth effects. No results bearing on V1–V6 are missing from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, convolutional networks, random or corrupted labels, and the stated size, optimizer, and training-duration conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, identity shortcuts, batch-normalized convolutional networks, plain tanh networks, and normalization-free residual networks.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation across layers, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and very deep plain networks.
Learning rates relative to a stability threshold, curvature or sharpness at that threshold, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: QIF (best)
rows.operation_detail: Exact spike-based gradient descent on SHD using time-to-first-spike coding.
rows.note: The measure is training accuracy on SHD, not training classification error on a listed claim benchmark.
rows.check: The reported 97.0 ± 0.5% training accuracy is correct, but SHD spiking networks do not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: LIF (best)
rows.operation_detail: Exact spike-based gradient descent on SHD using time-to-first-spike coding.
rows.note: Training accuracy remains below the QIF model's reported value; this is on SHD.
rows.check: The reported 83.5 ± 1.1% training accuracy is correct; lower accuracy than QIF does not establish a partial effect for any listed version.

rows.subject: LIF (async)
rows.operation_detail: Exact spike-based gradient descent on SHD with a selected asynchronous-output configuration.
rows.note: The paper reports this substantially lower training accuracy for the asynchronous LIF configuration.
rows.check: The reported 45.6 ± 1.8% training accuracy is correct; this asynchronous LIF condition does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: QIF (large)
rows.operation_detail: Exploratory training of a larger QIF network on SHD.
rows.note: Metrics are averaged over 9 runs with different seeds; no uncertainty type is specified for this value.
rows.check: The reported 99.973 ± 0.012% training accuracy is correct. Near-zero error in this SHD spiking network does not test V1's convolutional networks on CIFAR.

rows.subject: LIF (large)
rows.operation_detail: Exploratory training of a larger LIF network on SHD.
rows.note: Metrics are averaged over 9 runs with different seeds; no uncertainty type is specified for this value.
rows.check: The reported 94.08 ± 0.41% training accuracy is correct, but does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: QIF (best)
rows.operation_detail: Compared actual training-step loss changes with expected changes from the gradient.
rows.measure: Fraction of steps with expected loss decrease that actually decreased loss
rows.note: The comparison concerns the predictive accuracy of the gradient along the training trajectory.
rows.check: The 90% value is correct. It measures agreement between expected and actual loss changes, without testing curvature or a learning-rate stability threshold.

rows.subject: LIF (best)
rows.operation_detail: Compared actual training-step loss changes with expected changes from the gradient.
rows.measure: Fraction of steps with expected loss decrease that actually decreased loss
rows.note: The paper reports a lower fraction than for QIF.
rows.check: The 75% value is correct. Lower gradient predictiveness than QIF is not a partial effect for any listed version.

rows.operation_detail: Compared actual training-step loss changes with expected changes from the gradient.
rows.measure: Fraction of steps with expected loss decrease that actually decreased loss
rows.note: The paper reports a lower fraction than for QIF and the best-performing LIF model.
rows.check: The 62% value is correct. Lower gradient predictiveness does not measure any listed version.
